title_en: Philippines could be key player in US-China AI competition
content_en:
Manila is joining the scramble among Southeast Asian nations to attract hi-tech investment.
Illustration: Mario Cameira
“We’ve just consummated a trade deal, the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far and it’s a fair deal for both countries. … It’s a magnificent deal for both,” US President Donald Trump declared as he visited Manila this month. “I’m proud to say that we’re making the alliance between the United States and the Philippines much stronger than it’s ever been before, especially with the consummation of this deal.”
Days after Trump’s characteristically superlative pronouncement, however, there are still few details about the exact nature of the ostensibly new trade agreement. For instance, it’s not clear if it would lead to a significant reduction of US tariffs on Philippine exports and include a new energy deal. Confronting the prospect of stagflation, the Philippines is desperate for new trade and energy deals to revive its struggling economy.
What is clear is that the two allies didn’t sign the much-anticipated framework agreement under Pax Silica, the US-led geoeconomic plan aimed at creating a China-free supply chain for critical minerals, chips and other cutting-edge technologies.
“There is no signing. Not on this trip. We are not covering that on this trip,” Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr clarified to reporters. He has also insisted that there are no plans to set up resource-consuming AI data centres, which have provoked widespread protests in places including the United States. Nevertheless, the Philippine government remains committed to joining Pax Silica.
In competing with China, the US is desperate to gain access to critical minerals and strategic locations in places such as the Philippines. If anything, the latest US restrictions targeting Chinese companies’ access to cutting-edge semiconductors reveal Washington’s commitment to maintain the country’s dominance in artificial intelligence (AI).
In fairness, the US-China-Russia trilateral summit in Shenzhen, which took place right after Trump’s visit to Manila, was no empty gesture. The peace declaration issued by Trump, President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin emphasised their shared commitment to institutionalising an “open and candid” channel for discussing matters of global relevance, including energy security. Crucially, they reaffirmed their shared commitment to shunning any nuclear war, which “cannot be won and must never be fought”.
[embedded media]
Given the complexity and structural nature of tensions between the US, China and Russia, however, any major diplomatic breakthrough would require a level of strategic patience and dedication that a lame-duck Trump simply might not possess.
Great power competition in critical sectors is likely to intensify given that a new global governance architecture is unlikely to be created any time soon. This is especially true in the realm of AI, which has become a largely bipolar rivalry between the US and China. And for several reasons, no region is more central to this intensified rivalry than Southeast Asia.
One reason is geography. Southeast Asia is not only close to China’s industrial hub in the Pearl River Delta but also a critical node in the Japanese, South Korean, Taiwanese and Western supply chains. This places many regional states in a prize position to attract hi-tech investments, particularly with regard to semiconductor supply chains.
Another factor is natural resources, especially critical minerals. Indonesia and the Philippines, for instance, are among the world’s largest producers of nickel, which is vital to the production of semiconductor devices. Moreover, energy-rich Malaysia, which is positioning itself as Asia’s Silicon Valley, has the industrial and power-generating infrastructure to support massive AI data centres.
Workers lay cables outside Bridge Data Centres on May 6 in Johor state, Malaysia, which has become Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing data centre hub. Photo: Reuters
Southeast Asian nations from Vietnam to Thailand are also home to global industrial hubs. Meanwhile, Singapore has emerged as a global start-up and fintech hub, becoming a crucial pool of venture capital across the region. The recent scandal over Nvidia and Megaspeed is proof of the city state’s central role in the flow and regulation of semiconductors and other critical technologies.
Meanwhile, the Philippines is pursuing hi-tech investment from Western and traditional partners under the Pax Silica initiative. In spite of widespread criticism, especially from progressive groups bemoaning ecological risks and potential displacement of vulnerable groups, the Marcos administration is pressing ahead with joining Pax Silica as part of the country’s broader effort to boost growth and industrialise the economy.
Marcos allies in the legislature have filed the Advanced Industries Development Act. The bill aims to create a new ecosystem for the implementation of Pax Silica and other related initiatives, most notably the Luzon Economic Corridor, in tandem with Western partners.
Rich in resources and strategically located between major industrial powers, Manila is creating a new tech-industrial corridor from Clark to Cagayan, with a growing focus on critical minerals processing, semiconductor production and satellite launch sites. A key US ally, the Philippines is positioning itself as a trusted partner in the hope that it can catch up with its more industrialised peers.
An activist holds a picture of the decapitated head of US President Donald Trump during a protest at Liwasang Bonifacio against the Pax Silica initiative in Manila on November 17. Photo: Reuters
Though still ahead of China in terms of compute power and AI frontier labs, the US needs the fabrication capacity, critical minerals and the combined industrial base of its allies to effectively compete with Beijing. For its part, China hopes to rope more Southeast Asian nations into its own techno-industrial ecosystem through initiatives such as the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation.
But the Trump administration’s recent blacklisting of key Southeast Asian nations for chip exports on the one hand and aggressive pursuit of AI-centred initiatives with others like the Philippines on the other hand will put the region in an increasingly difficult position.
As they compete for hi-tech investment, regional states are likely to come under growing pressure to choose between rival AI regimes with serious consequences for their strategic autonomy. Welcome to the new “great game” in Asia.
By Richard Heydarian

title_en: Colombian Congress chiefs rush to reassure China as envoy berates lawmakers in Taiwan
content_en:
Foreign ministry also dropped Brics bank bid as Ambassador Zhu Jingyang quoted Confucius at the delegation hosted by Taiwan.
Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella has not yet commented on the Colombian lawmakers' trip to Taiwan. Photo: AFP
Colombian congressional leaders lined up to reaffirm the one-China policy in meetings with Beijing’s ambassador, as nine lawmakers neared the end of a trip to Taiwan that Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has yet to comment on.
On Thursday, Chinese Ambassador Zhu Jingyang met Elizabeth Jay-Pang Diaz, who chairs the Colombian government’s lower house foreign affairs committee, and the embassy said she reaffirmed the policy.
Earlier in the week, Zhu met speaker Nicolas Barguil and the chamber’s second vice-president Erick Velasco, and on Wednesday night he received lawmakers from former president Gustavo Petro’s left-wing Pacto Historico.
The flurry of meetings came after the embassy protested on Monday after a senator on the trip called Taipei’s representative in Bogota “ambassador”.
It described Taiwan as the “first insurmountable red line” in relations with Colombia. The nine Colombian travellers come from seven parties, from Pacto Historico to right-wing allies of De la Espriella.
[embedded media]
The government has said nothing publicly about the trip, and its position has emerged only through the Chinese embassy, which said Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula told Zhu over breakfast on Wednesday that Colombia’s adherence to the one-China policy, which Beijing refers to as a principle, “has never changed and will not change”.
Under the policy, countries with diplomatic ties to the People’s Republic must recognise it as China’s sole legitimate government and avoid official contacts with Taiwan, which it claims as its territory.
Bula’s ministry announced the same day that Colombia would drop Petro’s bid to join the Brics group and its New Development Bank, which involved a US$512.5 million capital subscription. The statement did not explain why.
Since taking office in August, De la Espriella has moved Colombia closer to Washington, and two days before his inauguration US ambassador nominee Nate Morris told a Senate hearing that the president-elect had committed to pulling out of China’s Belt and Road Initiative – which aims to improve trade and economic integration across Asia, Europe and Africa – though no withdrawal has been announced.
The shift fits a regional policy that runs on a separate track from US President Donald Trump’s courting of Xi Jinping, whom he met in Shenzhen last week for their third summit this year.
While Trump boasts of “fantastic relationships” with Xi, his administration has pressed Latin American governments to scale back Chinese involvement under a modified Monroe Doctrine that treats the region as Washington’s sphere of influence.
Senator Agmeth Escaf of Pacto Historico, who is on the trip, demanded respect after the ambassador called the lawmakers “inept”, and on Wednesday afternoon Zhu answered with a post quoting Confucius.
“To those who ask me for absolute and unconditional respect for those Colombian congressmen who commit the grave error of improper interference in China’s internal affairs with their trip to Taiwan, this is my answer,” he wrote.
“Respect is earned with respect. Those who do not respect and offend first do not deserve our respect, full stop.”
He added in a second post that Confucius rejected repaying evil with kindness “because then there would be no way left to respond to true kindness”.
Escaf wrote back in an open letter that calling legislators “inept” and “manipulated” was not becoming of an accredited diplomat. “From me you will never receive an insult,” he said.
Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed by law to supplying it with weapons.
Lunch with Taiwan’s foreign minister
Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung hosted the delegation, which was led by lower house first vice-president Simon Molina, for lunch on Wednesday in Taipei.
Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung met the Colombian delegation for lunch on Wednesday. Photo: CNA
Molina told him he would promote policies to ease travel and trade with Taiwan after returning home, according to Taiwan’s foreign ministry. Lin said he hoped more Colombian coffee and cocoa would reach Taiwan.
In Bogota that evening, Zhu described his meetings with Barguil and Velasco as “dialogue in mutual respect” with Colombia’s legislature, “the honourable House of Representatives included”.
On Thursday, the embassy turned on the Taipei Commercial Office in Bogota, calling it “a political farce” and warning Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party that “those who play with fire will end up getting burned”.
The office rejected the accusations and said parliamentary visits were a “customary form of exchange”.
China is Colombia’s second-largest trading partner after the United States. Bogota switched diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing in 1980, and seven of the 12 countries that still recognise Taiwan are in Latin America and the Caribbean.
Colombian lawmakers have been to Taipei at least three times since September last year.
On the second of those trips, the chairs of both chambers’ foreign affairs committees told Lin they would push for Colombia to reopen an office on the self-governing island, and Petro’s foreign ministry disowned the remarks the next day.
By Igor Patrick

title_en: Ukraine says it used laser weapon to shoot down Russian drone for first time
content_en:
The system was used to intercept a Geran jet drone, which is faster and harder to bring down than earlier models.
Journalists stand next to an unexploded Russian Geran-4 drone displayed in Kyiv, Ukraine, in October. Photo: AP
Ukraine has for the first time used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered drone, its state-backed defence group Brave1 said on Friday.
Earlier this week, Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky, published footage showing a target crashing in a fireball, saying a Russian Geran jet drone had been shot down by a laser system for the “first time”.
“Footage recently emerged online showing a Ukrainian laser system being used in combat to intercept an enemy jet-powered drone,” Brave1 said.
The weapon was developed by a recipient of a Brave1 grant and operated by a private air defence team, it added.
But Brave1 cautioned that “a first successful interception does not mean the technology is ready for mass deployment”.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul look at a Russian Geran-2 drone in Kyiv in August. Photo: Press Service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine via Reuters
“Laser air defence remains an experimental technology,” it said, adding at least seven teams in Ukraine were currently working on laser weapons.
Zelensky’s adviser Beskrestnov said the system, known as Blysk and developed by Carmine Sky, was protecting critical infrastructure during the interception.
Ukraine has faced near-daily barrages of Russian drones and missiles throughout the war.
In recent months, Moscow has increasingly deployed jet drones, which are faster and harder to bring down than earlier models.
According to Brave1, laser weapons have been in development since the 1970s but are operational in only a handful of countries.
Successful combat shoot-downs of airborne targets with the technology are still rare.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Canada’s top court upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
content_en:
Rights groups warn that the ruling unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.
The Supreme Court of Canada in seen in Ottawa on Friday. Photo: The Canadian Press via AP
Canada’s Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec’s ban on religious symbols for public servants, prompting rights groups to warn the ruling unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.
The decision is a political win for Quebec’s sovereigntist government and could complicate Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to unify Canada as the country faces a trade war and annexation threats from US President Donald Trump.
Quebec’s ‌previous government passed Bill 21 in 2019, saying it was necessary to protect its secularist society.
Under the law, anyone receiving services from public servants like teachers and police officers in the predominantly French-speaking province has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.
Quebec used an unusual constitutional provision to shield the law from court challenges, which the Supreme Court decided was allowed.
Joe Ortona, chair of the English Montreal School Board, responds to the ruling on Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, at the Supreme Court of Canada in Ottawa on Friday. Photo: The Canadian Press via AP
In its ruling, Canada’s top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, saying it is “rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society”.
The Supreme Court found, however, that one provision of the bill infringed the ⁠rights of members of Quebec’s National Assembly whose religious beliefs require them to wear a face covering.
The ruling drew condemnation from some groups.
“This decision is an unrestricted licence for every government ‌in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian,” said Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims.
He said the law had forced many Muslim women – who wear a head covering as part of their faith – to ‌stop working as teachers and that some could no longer be volunteers at their children’s schools.
Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, ⁠described the law as “Islamophobia as a state policy”.
Quebec ⁠is Canada’s only majority-French speaking province and has numerous laws guaranteeing the primacy of the French language and Carney has repeatedly said protecting Quebecois culture is a matter of Canadian sovereignty.
Quebec’s bill aligns with the French tradition of ‌state secularism, although Quebec’s rules are much narrower than those in France.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks with reporters before a meeting on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Wednesday. Photo: The Canadian Press via AP
“Unlike the rest of Canada, where there is a greater acceptance of all expressions of religious belief, here in Quebec, we have a certain mistrust about the right to ‌express religion, ‌mostly because they are a reminder of a time when religion was extremely influential in political institutions,” said Patrick Taillon, a professor of constitutional law at Laval University in Quebec City.
Kerri Froc, an associate professor at the University of New Brunswick who focuses on women’s constitutional rights, said Canada’s top court had set a worrying precedent in refusing to limit ⁠the powers of provinces as long as they invoke the unusual constitutional provision.
“The Supreme Court has sent a clear message it’s not going to step in when the rights of ⁠vulnerable minorities are trampled on in these cases, so perhaps this needs to move to the political sphere,” Froc said.
Alberta, Ontario and Saskatchewan have all used the same provision that Quebec relied on for its bill to pass legislation in recent years on issues like transgender policies and to end strikes.
In a post on social media, ‌Mathieu Levesque, interim leader of the Coalition Avenir Quebec (CAQ), ‌the Quebec provincial party that passed Bill 21, said the ruling was “a victory for the Quebec nation and the CAQ”.
Carney told reporters the government respected the independence of the Supreme Court and was reviewing the decision. He called Canada “a mosaic” that was stronger when “everyone has an opportunity to thrive and flourish within their identities”.
Carney said his government would not use a constitutional provision that allows authorities to violate fundamental rights and would “always do what we can to protect those rights and liberties”.
“It’s a responsibility for the government and all legislators to protect minorities and diversity,” he said.
By Reuters

Quebec’s ‌previous government passed Bill 21 in 2019, saying it was necessary to protect its secularist society.
Under the law, anyone receiving services from public servants like teachers and police officers in the predominantly French-speaking province has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.
Quebec used an unusual constitutional provision to shield the law from court challenges, which the Supreme Court decided was allowed.
Joe Ortona, chair of the English Montreal School Board, responds to the ruling on Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, at the Supreme Court of Canada in Ottawa on Friday. Photo: The Canadian Press via AP
In its ruling, Canada’s top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, saying it is “rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society”.
The Supreme Court found, however, that one provision of the bill infringed the ⁠rights of members of Quebec’s National Assembly whose religious beliefs require them to wear a face covering.
The ruling drew condemnation from some groups.
“This decision is an unrestricted licence for every government ‌in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian,” said Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims.
He said the law had forced many Muslim women – who wear a head covering as part of their faith – to ‌stop working as teachers and that some could no longer be volunteers at their children’s schools.
Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, ⁠described the law as “Islamophobia as a state policy”.
Quebec ⁠is Canada’s only majority-French speaking province and has numerous laws guaranteeing the primacy of the French language and Carney has repeatedly said protecting Quebecois culture is a matter of Canadian sovereignty.
Quebec’s bill aligns with the French tradition of ‌state secularism, although Quebec’s rules are much narrower than those in France.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks with reporters before a meeting on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Wednesday. Photo: The Canadian Press via AP
“Unlike the rest of Canada, where there is a greater acceptance of all expressions of religious belief, here in Quebec, we have a certain mistrust about the right to ‌express religion, ‌mostly because they are a reminder of a time when religion was extremely influential in political institutions,” said Patrick Taillon, a professor of constitutional law at Laval University in Quebec City.
Kerri Froc, an associate professor at the University of New Brunswick who focuses on women’s constitutional rights, said Canada’s top court had set a worrying precedent in refusing to limit ⁠the powers of provinces as long as they invoke the unusual constitutional provision.
“The Supreme Court has sent a clear message it’s not going to step in when the rights of ⁠vulnerable minorities are trampled on in these cases, so perhaps this needs to move to the political sphere,” Froc said.
Alberta, Ontario and Saskatchewan have all used the same provision that Quebec relied on for its bill to pass legislation in recent years on issues like transgender policies and to end strikes.
In a post on social media, ‌Mathieu Levesque, interim leader of the Coalition Avenir Quebec (CAQ), ‌the Quebec provincial party that passed Bill 21, said the ruling was “a victory for the Quebec nation and the CAQ”.
Carney told reporters the government respected the independence of the Supreme Court and was reviewing the decision. He called Canada “a mosaic” that was stronger when “everyone has an opportunity to thrive and flourish within their identities”.
Carney said his government would not use a constitutional provision that allows authorities to violate fundamental rights and would “always do what we can to protect those rights and liberties”.
“It’s a responsibility for the government and all legislators to protect minorities and diversity,” he said.

title_en: WHO sounds alarm as measles fight falters: ‘it is back’
content_en:
Vaccines chief Kate O’Brien cited the US losing its measles elimination status as a stark reminder of how quickly diseases can resurface.
Information material on measles is displayed at Chester County Health Department in West Chester, Pennsylvania, on Tuesday. Photo: AFP
The World Health Organization sounded the alarm on measles on Friday, warning that progress on elimination had stalled amid rising misinformation and disinformation.
The WHO’s overview of the long-term battle against the highly contagious disease came the week after the United States lost its measles elimination status, with declining vaccination rates sending US cases soaring.
Worldwide, the Covid-19 pandemic disrupted immunisation programmes, the UN health agency said, with many countries struggling to get vaccine coverage back up to pre-pandemic levels – and to reach those missed during the crisis.
WHO vaccines chief Kate O’Brien said the US situation was a stark reminder of how quickly preventable diseases can resurface when immunisation coverage falls.
“Are we ringing the alarm bell about the number of children who are unvaccinated or under-vaccinated? Absolutely. Measles is the most infectious virus known to humans,” she told a press conference from the WHO’s Geneva headquarters.
“It is back – and the world is learning just how sick and just how dead measles can make you.”
[embedded media]
Measles causes fever, respiratory symptoms and skin rashes. In some cases, it can lead to pneumonia and inflammation of the brain, potentially causing lasting damage or death.
It is most common in children, who are typically offered two doses of vaccine by the time they reach 18 months old.
“Progress has stalled in recent years,” the WHO said.
Global estimated coverage with a first dose of measles vaccine remained stable in 2025 at 84 per cent compared to the year before – down from the pre-pandemic level of 86 per cent in 2019, the agency said.
Coverage with the second dose of measles vaccine remained at an all-time high of 77 per cent in 2025, with more countries having introduced second jabs.
Gabon and the Central African Republic are the only two WHO member states yet to bring a second dose into routine immunisation schedules.
The WHO says at least 95 per cent coverage with two doses is required to stop transmission and protect communities.
An estimated 20.8 million children went unvaccinated in 2025, while a further 8.3 million were left on only one dose.
Although the percentage of unvaccinated children remained stable, the raw number went up due to the increase in the number of newborn babies.
People line up for vaccines in Mexico City on Thursday. Photo: AFP
The outbreak in the US is its worst in over three decades, with more than 5,400 cases reported this year.
Medical experts have accused health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jnr, a noted vaccine sceptic, of fanning distrust in vaccinations by repeatedly highlighting unfounded safety concerns.
O’Brien said misinformation and disinformation were “a significant contributor” to leaving parents “confused about what they should be doing”.
“Vaccines have, in many places, gotten tangled up with political polarisation or ideological polarisation,” she said.
As for taking children to so-called measles parties to catch the virus as a means of immunisation, “exposing children to measles is a terrible idea”, O’Brien stressed.
“I really want to dispel this idea that measles is some rite of passage of childhood. It’s not. It’s a serious illness for which we have a safe and effective vaccine.”
A vial containing the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) combination vaccine is displayed in West Chester, Pennsylvania, on Tuesday. Photo: AFP
Measles vaccination since 2000 is estimated to have saved more than 60 million lives – more than any other childhood immunisation over the past 50 years, O’Brien added.
WHO modelling provides estimates that there were around 9.8 million measles cases and a historic low of 72,000 measles deaths last year.
Case numbers are down from a figure of 37.8 million in 2000.
A total of 59 countries experienced large or disruptive outbreaks in 2025, including 28 in the African region and 13 in Europe.
Eleven of the 59 countries were currently or previously verified as having eliminated measles.
A total of 92 countries have been verified as having achieved or maintained measles elimination.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: More than 57,000 granted UK permanent residence via BN(O) route in year to September
content_en:
UK Home Office says many of the earliest cohorts from Hong Kong have now completed the required five-year period of continuous residence.
According to the UK Home Office, 57,040 people were granted permanent residence via the BN(O) route in the 12 months to September 30. Photo: Xinhua
More than 57,000 arrivals from Hong Kong became permanent residents in the United Kingdom in the 12 months to September 2026 under the bespoke BN(O) immigration pathway launched five years ago, with the city ranking second behind India in the number of UK settlement grants during the period.
According to the UK Home Office, 57,040 people were granted permanent residence via the BN(O) route in the 12 months to September 30, 2026.
This was up from just 637 BN(O) grants in the preceding 12 months and represented almost a quarter of all permanent residencies granted during the period.
Introduced in 2021, the BN(O) route allows applicants and their dependents to live, work and study in the United Kingdom for up to five years.
After living in the UK for five years, BN(O) visa holders can apply to stay permanently under “indefinite leave to remain”, which gives them the right to live, work or study in the UK permanently and to apply for government benefits. They can then apply for British citizenship one year after being granted leave to remain.
“The route has now reached the point where many of the earliest cohorts have completed the five-year qualifying period of continuous residence required for settlement in the UK,” the UK Home Office said.
A BN(O) passport. Photo: Fung Chang
Settlement grants to people recorded by the Home Office as being from Hong Kong, including some who arrived via the BN(O) route, also increased substantially, rising from 760 in the year ending September 2025 to 31,703 in the following 12 months – the second largest group after the 44,793 Indian passport holders granted settlement during the period.
Settlement grants to people recorded by the Home Office as being from mainland China also increased, rising from 5,506 to 31,042. This also included some people who settled via the BN(O) route.
“These increases reflected that BN(O) visa holders completed the qualifying period of continuous residence required for settlement,” it added.
The Home Office also said that the number of applications for BN(O) visas continued to decline.
“BN(O) out-of-country visas peaked in the year ending March 2022, with 86,439 granted, soon after the scheme opened,” it said.
“BN(O) visa grants have decreased each year since. There were 5,146 grants of BN(O) visas in the year ending September 2026, bringing the total number of grants to 189,347 since the scheme opened.”
The BN(O) scheme was introduced in response to Beijing’s imposition of the national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.
The legislation, which prohibits acts of secession, subversion, terrorism and collusion with foreign forces, followed months of anti-government protests in 2019.
By Cannix Yau

title_en: Chinese heavy-machinery giants XCMG, Sany deploy driverless, electric fleets in global push
content_en:
Chinese giants bank on robust supply chain and local robotics advances to take on Caterpillar and Komatsu in mining, construction sectors.
A 400-ton electric mining excavator is displayed at the Sany booth during the Bauma China 2026 exhibition in Shanghai on November 24. Photo: VCG via Getty Images
China’s two largest construction machinery makers, XCMG and Sany, have doubled down on automation technologies to expand their overseas sales in an effort to disrupt the global pecking order.
Banking on China’s complete supply chain and technological advancements in robotics, both industrial juggernauts could produce driverless, fully electric fleets used in mining and construction to take on the likes of Caterpillar and Komatsu, according to company executives.
“We are showing unmanned, clustered operations across the entire process of excavation, loading, transport, paving and rolling,” Yang Dongsheng, chairman of state-owned XCMG, said at the Bauma China 2026 trade show in Shanghai on Tuesday. “Through a deepened integration of equipment fitted with embodied artificial intelligence technology in a smart control system, XCMG can provide our customers with a fleet of fully autonomous machines to improve efficiency.”
Bauma China, Asia’s largest trade fair for construction machinery and the mining industry, drew more than 4,000 exhibitors from about 30 countries and regions, the organisers said. The four-day event was expected to attract 300,000 visitors.
On Tuesday, XCMG signed a memorandum of understanding with Brazilian iron ore mining giant Vale to deepen their ties in the development of smart new-energy mining equipment.
The XCMG booth at the Bauma China 2026 trade show in Shanghai. Photo: Handout
Under the partnership, XCMG agreed to develop new machinery to help Vale optimise its cost of ownership, while testing next-generation large equipment such as hydraulic excavators at the Brazilian firm’s mining fields.
Sany, also an exhibitor at the trade fair, said AI technologies had enabled it to develop fully autonomous trucks and paving fleets to enhance its competitiveness in the international markets.
“Sany pavers and rollers without cabs can already work as one fleet,” the company said in a statement. “Since 2019, our driverless paving fleets, the world’s first in commercial use at scale, have logged more than 5,000 kilometres across more than 60 projects. One human operator with a tablet supervises up to 15 machines.”
Chinese manufacturers of construction equipment, electric vehicles (EVs) and electronic gadgets have revved up the pace of their global expansion in the past two years, propelled by technological and cost advantages.
Most have strengthened technological innovation in the past decade through better use of digital technologies and, more recently, AI, to reinforce their go-global drive.
XCMG, based in Xuzhou, eastern China’s Jiangsu province, ranked third globally in terms of sales last year, trailing Caterpillar and Komatsu, according to industry data provider KHL Group. Sany, headquartered in Changsha, capital of central China’s Hunan province, was sixth.
XCMG held a 5.8 per cent share of the US$246.6 billion global construction machinery market last year, while Sany’s share was 5.1 per cent, KHL data showed.
A visitor tries out a robotic excavator simulator from XCMG at the World Intelligent Manufacturing Expo held in Nanjing, east China’s Jiangsu Province, on November 19, 2026. Photo: Xinhua
In the first six months of 2026, China’s exports of excavators and other heavy machinery climbed 33.5 per cent to 73,295 units, according to data from the China Construction Machinery Association.
KHL said half of the output of Chinese construction machinery giants was shipped abroad in the first half as they pursued new growth opportunities amid a slowing domestic economy.
XCMG and Sany also build battery-powered heavy-duty trucks to bolster overseas sales.
S&P Global Ratings said in a report in June that Chinese firms were likely to increase their global market share as electric-powered trucks appeal to foreign buyers due to their low ownership costs.
XCMG and Sany have outperformed most conventional manufacturers of diesel-powered machines in the electric heavy-duty truck market over the past two years, the rating agency said.
By Daniel Ren

title_en: Chinese tourist region Guangxi proposes longer weekends as local economy grows just 2.5%
content_en:
Local officials are proposing a series of measures to boost travel and household spending, including a monthly 2.5-day weekend.
Aerial view of tourists taking bamboo rafts to tour the Yulong River in Yangshuo county, Guilin city, Guangxi, China. Photo: Getty Images
China’s southern Guangxi region, home to the dramatic karst peaks around Guilin, is considering giving workers more time off work in an effort to encourage local tourism and boost consumer spending.
A draft plan released for public comment by the regional Department of Culture and Tourism encouraged eligible employers to offer a 2.5-day weekend once a month to increase the number of short trips in the region.
While other Chinese provinces have tested flexible time-off arrangements, Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region is the first to propose a monthly schedule.
The 16-point plan also called for promoting shorter trips to less popular tourist destinations, alongside night markets, hotels, immersive live performances and bundled events. It proposed subsidies of up to 5 million yuan (US$750,000) for new shops and attractions inside parks.
Education authorities would be urged to arrange two to four days off for primary and secondary school students in both spring and autumn, according to the proposal, encouraging family travel.
The plan comes as Guangxi’s economy grew just 2.5 per cent in the first three quarters of 2026, below the national rate of 4.6 per cent. Retail sales also fell 0.1 per cent, against a 1.1 per cent increase nationwide. Tourism, along with manufacturing, agriculture and cross-border trade, drives the regional economy.
But some analysts questioned whether extra time off work would raise tourism spending, given tight household budgets and the challenge of enforcing leave arrangements in the private sector. The draft also omitted details on which employers and workers would qualify, or how workplaces should adjust schedules.
Liu Kaiming, a labour researcher and founder of the Shenzhen-based Institute of Contemporary Observation, warned that the policy could widen the gap in leave entitlements. “For civil servants and public institutions, the policy could mean additional benefits that are difficult for private-sector workers to access,” he said.
Liu also questioned whether local residents had the disposable income to travel more. “You can give people more time off, but if they don’t have the money, how can they travel?” he said.
Wu Shouping, deputy director of the urban development research institute at the Nanning Academy of Social Sciences, suggested trialling the plan at selected workplaces, with childcare support and other measures to help ease the burden on employers and government.
That way, the time-off scheme could translate into sustained spending on local tourism, Wu added.
Wu also suggested that regional officials promote local tourist attractions, access to the Pinglu Canal – a 134.2km (83.4 mile) waterway in Guangxi – and destinations near the border with Southeast Asia, Wu said.
By He Huifeng

title_en: In Southeast Asia, China’s split personality stands out
content_en:
Beijing wields major creditor and industrial clout while claiming developing-world kinship, creating regional friction.
China’s Premier Li Qiang (sixth from left) and Southeast Asian delegates at the Asean-China summit on November 16. Photo: AP
Countries, like people, can have several identities at once. They are a source of strength, but also of tension when different identities pull in different directions. China is reaching that point, with Southeast Asia confronting growing gaps between the Global South identity that Beijing claims, the great-power capabilities it wields and the expectations placed on it as an emerging global leader.
China describes itself as the world’s largest developing country. The claim partially holds given the wide developmental disparities within China and its per capita income remaining well below that of advanced economies. But China is also the world’s second-largest economy, a technological leader across a widening range of industries and a major creditor. It is a great power that increasingly wields the chokepoints its industrial dominance has created and asserts a predominant role in its own neighbourhood.
The recent Apec summit in Shenzhen put these tensions on full display. As host, and as a major beneficiary of an open global economy, China presented itself as a defender of multilateralism and the rules-based trading system. Yet the political spectacle of the Trump-Xi-Putin summit overshadowed the multilateral gathering. China was at once championing an inclusive regional order while claiming a central place in an exclusive three-way conversation that projected the opposite: an international order managed among great powers, reviving anxieties about spheres of influence and a might-makes-right world.
Chinese President Xi Jinping (centre) welcomes his American and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin for the Apec summit in Shenzhen on November 18. Photo: dpa
For smaller states, this exposes an underlying tension in China’s diplomacy. Beijing advocates greater democracy and justice in international relations, where the voice of the majority counts. Yet it also operates within a great-power logic, in which a few powers negotiate the terms of order.
The same tension runs through China’s economic engagement abroad. Inequality in global governance no longer falls neatly along the developed-developing divide. It increasingly exists within the Global South, including between China and many of the countries whose interests it claims to champion.
As China grows wealthier and positions itself as a champion of global governance reform, and as the US retreats from global leadership, expectations of Beijing are changing. Take development finance. Will China provide more grants and concessional assistance instead of relying predominantly on loans? Will it assume a greater share of the burden when heavily indebted countries run into financial distress?
China does not see itself as another Western-style donor giving aid to poorer countries. It frames its engagement as South-South cooperation among equals. Yet its role as a major creditor to far smaller economies creates a stark asymmetry. Nearly half of Laos’ external public debt is owed to China and the Southeast Asian nation’s financial distress has led to a growing Chinese foothold in its strategic infrastructure: China Southern Power Grid now holds a 90 per cent stake in the joint venture that manages Laos’ high-voltage grid. This illustrates how cooperation framed around equality and mutual benefit can, under conditions of deep asymmetry, reinforce the stronger partner’s leverage.
A high-speed train leaves a station on the Jakarta-Bandung high-speed railway in Bandung, Indonesia, in May 2025. Photo: Xinhua
Indonesia confronts the debt issue at the project level. The Jakarta-Bandung high-speed railway cost US$7.27 billion, about 75 per cent of it financed by China Development Bank loans. Conceived as a business-to-business venture, the financial burden ultimately fell on the state – with Jakarta now seeking to stretch its repayments to Beijing over decades.
When the economics underpinning Chinese lending falter, development finance gives way to negotiations over who bears the costs. Beijing has shown flexibility through deferrals and restructuring, but the underlying financial burden largely remains with the borrower, as the debt is deferred, not forgiven. This sharpens the tension between China’s identity as a fellow developing country and the greater forbearance increasingly expected of it as a major creditor with vastly greater financial capacity.
Industrialisation presents another facet of the tension.
For decades, East Asia’s development was described through the “flying geese” model. As the lead goose moved into more sophisticated industries, lower-value production migrated to those following behind: from Japan to the newly industrialised economies, then to China and Southeast Asia.
China does not fit neatly into this pattern. It now leads in electric vehicles, batteries, solar technology, telecommunications and sophisticated machinery, yet has not vacated the lower and middle rungs of manufacturing. This creates a tension between China’s economic interests and its neighbours’ developmental aspirations.
Chinese firms have strong incentives to move production to Southeast Asia, from where they can reach growing markets, pay lower wages and better navigate US tariffs. But the Chinese government also has compelling reasons to resist the hollowing-out of its industrial base, given concerns over employment and economic security.
Shein’s office in Guangzhou. China’s Commerce Ministry reportedly discouraged Shein from shifting more sourcing and production overseas. Photo: Kyodo
In 2025, Beijing reportedly tightened transfers of specialised manufacturing equipment and technical personnel to India and Southeast Asia, seeking to limit the movement of manufacturing capacity and know-how abroad. China’s Commerce Ministry also reportedly discouraged Shein from shifting more sourcing and production overseas. Combined with AI-enabled automation, China’s vast industrial ecosystem may ultimately allow it to remain competitive across multiple rungs of the value chain all at once.
Here too, China’s identities pull apart. As a Global South leader, it speaks the language of shared development, but its domestic economic imperatives give it reasons to protect its own industrial base. This opens a gap between what partners expect of the “lead goose”, which is to make room for those behind, and what they actually experience. For members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the central question is whether deeper integration with China leaves enough room for their own industrial upgrading.
Reconciling these tensions will require more than skilful strategic communication from Beijing. China’s multiple identities are real, and so are the tensions among them. Its Global South identity is important to its political positioning, but its growing capabilities increasingly make it think and act as a great power.
Southeast Asia will therefore judge China not simply by the identity it claims but by how it uses its power: whether it assumes greater responsibilities, leaves space for others to prosper and exercises restraint when it holds the stronger hand.
Hoang Thi Ha is Senior Fellow and Co-coordinator of the Regional Strategic and Political Studies Programme at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.

title_en: China’s ‘national team’ isn’t riding to save A-share investors
content_en:
Readers discuss the dangers of a rescue-dependent mindset, and the benefits of just 10 minutes of expressive writing.
A delivery worker rides a scooter past the Shenzhen Stock Exchange in Shenzhen on November 17. Photo: Reuters
Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words.
Every time A-shares plunge, investors turn to a single prayer: when is the “national team” stepping in? Most assume stabilisation funds will automatically catch the fall. Yet a decade of rescue history reveals a brutal truth: if you wait for the national team to buy, you’ve already missed the initial turn – and by the time the real market bottom forms, most investors are too trapped in pessimism to act.
Stabilisation funds exist to extinguish systemic risk, not bail out cyclical dips. Their core objective is halting liquidity feedback loops and preventing financial crashes. They will not rescue capital trapped mid-decline, as doing so would tie up state capital at inflated levels. A genuine mid-to-long-term bottom must be forged through the market’s own spontaneous deleveraging.
A distinct time lag separates the “policy bottom” from the “market bottom”, often accompanied by a gruelling secondary drawdown: in 2008, a 40-day gap between the September policy bottom and October market bottom; in 2015, a six-month grind downward after China Securities Finance capital entered in July; in 2018 and 2022, consistent two-to-six-month intervals where indices endured an additional 10 per cent to 20 per cent downside.
Policy capital can halt panic-driven collapses, but it cannot instantly reverse earnings pressures or macroeconomic trends. Treating state intervention as a direct buy signal is misguided. Stabilisation funds act as multi-year ballast capital with near-infinite patience. Retail investors, burdened by strict time constraints and psychological pressure, often crack during the bottom-grinding phase and cut losses at the worst possible time.
Additionally, recurring emergency market rescues distort the market ecosystem. Constant interventions foster moral hazard, reinforcing retail investors’ wishful thinking that policy will always save them, ultimately amplifying long-term volatility.
For everyday investors, success requires stepping out of the rescue-dependent mindset. Maintain sensible position sizing, build in substantial safety margins, and evaluate holdings strictly on earnings stability, valuation and cash flow health. A mature market relies on pricing discipline, not training wheels. The ultimate edge isn’t guessing Beijing’s next move – it is holding assets so fundamentally sound that you no longer care who is buying the index.
Yuxuan (Jack) Guo, Central
Students can turn to writing to clear the mind
As preparations for next year’s Diploma of Secondary Education exam intensify, Hong Kong’s Form 6 students would need more than sufficient rest to deal with stress. In a survey released earlier this year by the Hong Kong Federation of Youth Groups, nearly half of the Form 6 students surveyed already reported high stress – a full year before they sit the exam.
In fact, schools have a cheap, well-evidenced tool here that most of them are not using, which is expressive writing. In 2011, Gerardo Ramirez and Sian Beilock of the University of Chicago reported in Science that students who spent 10 minutes writing freely about their worries just before a major exam did better than expected.
Among highly anxious students, the exercise broke the usual link between anxiety and lower scores. Worry takes up mental space that students need for solving problems, and putting it on paper seems to free some of that space. A wider body of research on expressive writing points the same way.
This fits what I have seen in years of exploring what I call blog psychology: people often understand their stress better once they put it into sentences.
None of this needs a new programme. Form teachers could set aside 10 minutes a week for private writing, with no marking and no sharing. Schools could give candidates a few quiet minutes with a sheet of paper before mock exams, so the routine feels familiar before the real thing. Parents could resist reading what their children write and simply ask what worries them most, then listen.
Writing is not counselling, and it will not fix a system in which one set of exams can feel like a verdict on a whole life. Ten minutes and a sheet of paper are a small thing to offer. Schools that try it can judge for themselves whether it helps.
Dennis Relojo-Howell, London, UK

title_en: Should AI really be a matter of national security?
content_en:
History argues that tech transfer is inevitable and a more cooperative approach between nations is better for everyone.
A professor holds a silicon wafer as students from Rio Salado College participate in a chip making lab at the Arizona State University NanoFab in Tempe, Arizona, on October 20. Photo: AP
In 1810, France granted citizenship to William Cockerill, an English mechanic and engineer, for helping to turn what is today Belgium – beginning near Liege – into one of Europe’s first regions to industrialise after Britain.
By today’s standards, Cockerill was engaged in industrial espionage and illegal technology transfer. Though no secret agent, he defied strict British laws that barred skilled artisans from emigrating and from taking industrial secrets, machine models and designs with them.
Around 1819, Franz Anton Egells, a Westphalian locksmith, was sent by Prussia to Britain, ostensibly for technical training. Since Britain barred foreigners from sensitive factories, he had to work incognito in restricted machine shops, memorising designs and secretly sketching components. On his return, he set up Berlin’s first major machine-building works with state support and became a model for later German industrialists.
In the first half of the 19th century, others made similar trips, illegal or merely questionable. Among them were Alfred Krupp, who became one of Germany’s most important industrialists and arms makers, and the Dutch manufacturer Paul van Vlissingen, who helped lay the foundations of industrialisation in the Netherlands.
Tsar Alexander II made the German merchant Ludwig Knoop a Russian baron for building up the country’s cotton industry by importing British machines and skilled personnel after Britain lifted its ban on such machinery exports in 1843.
Samuel Slater, who brought British textile technology to the United States in the late 18th century, was hailed by president Andrew Jackson as the “Father of the American Industrial Revolution”. In Britain, he was rather less celebrated and known as “Slater the Traitor”. Tench Coxe, assistant to America’s first treasury secretary Alexander Hamilton, promoted bounties and protection to lure foreign artisans who had industrial improvements and secrets to offer.
A statue of Alexander Hamilton stands in front of the US Treasury Department on January 18, 2023, in Washington. Hamilton was in favour of rewarding those who brought “improvements and secrets of extraordinary value” into the United States. Photo: Getty Images/TNS
Like the US today, Britain fiercely guarded its technologies as an industrial pioneer, punishing violators with fines, imprisonment and the loss of nationality and property. None of this stopped other Western nations from learning to industrialise from Britain by means fair and foul.
Yet the spread of its technologies helped create a new world economy in which Britain emerged as the pre-eminent industrial power of the age, far ahead of its European rivals and the young United States. A rising tide, after all, lifts all boats. As economic historian Sven Beckert wrote in Capitalism: A Global History, “by 1830 Britain dominated world manufacturing in ways comparable only to US domination after 1945 and Chinese domination in the first decades of the twenty-first century”.
Technology transfer and diffusion are inevitable. Britain failed to protect itself against intellectual property theft and industrial espionage, but it can be argued that this hardly mattered.
For students of economic and technological history, the Nvidia affair – the espionage allegations that led to CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and subsequent reinstatement – along with debates over open versus proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) and tech curbs, must bring a sense of deja vu. The US-China rivalry over AI essentially replays the old debate between free trade and protectionism.
On one side stands Huang, who advocates a more cooperative relationship between the two countries. On the other is Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who takes an almost neoconservative hard line on China and makes American national security an AI priority.
[embedded media]
Whether US technology curbs on China benefit the American economy is debatable. The short-term costs are clear; the long-term strategic gains are uncertain.
Chipmakers face lost sales, cancelled orders and writedowns when restrictions block shipments or disrupt demand. For example, Nvidia booked a US$400 million charge in the first half of fiscal 2027 for excess inventory of its H200 chips and purchase obligations amid licensing and import hurdles.
Curbs also accelerate Chinese self-reliance. Research from Harvard Business School found that earlier US export controls pushed sanctioned Chinese firms to raise R&D spending and patenting, reducing reliance on foreign technology. Hardware limits have likewise pushed Chinese developers towards efficiency techniques such as model compression and mixture-of-experts architectures.
Shifting rules, licensing requirements and third-country enforcement, such as tighter scrutiny of transshipments via Southeast Asia, add compliance costs and risk eroding global trust in US technology supply chains. Beijing has responded with export limits on gallium, germanium and rare earth magnets, as well as regulatory scrutiny of American firms. The curbs have also ensnared companies from allied countries, such as the Dutch chip equipment maker ASML.
At home, the hyperscalers’ outsize, increasingly debt-financed investments and heavy concentration in AI have skewed the American economy and fed fears of an investment bubble.
If history is any guide, a technological monopoly is short-lived. Eventually, everyone catches up. There is a strong case for cooperation on technology and AI.
By Alex Lo

title_en: India finds unsafe Bisleri sample due to bacteria amid bottled water crackdown
content_en:
Authorities have previously found a sample of Bisleri-branded water unsafe due to the presence of chemicals that may cause cancer.
Bisleri packaged drinking water bottles for sale at a refreshment drinks shop in Kolkata, India. Photo: Reuters
Indian authorities have found a sample of Bisleri-branded water to be unsafe due to coliform bacteria, a regulatory document shows, the second such finding to come to light in recent days on the nation’s biggest ‌and most popular packaged-water brand.
Bisleri’s 20-US cent bottles have made the company a household name in India, where poor water quality has turned bottled water into a necessity for homes and restaurants. It has remained the market leader while competing with PepsiCo and Coca-Cola in India’s US$3.5 billion packaged drinking-water market.
Consumer worries were already heightened in India after the food regulator said this week it had found a sample of Bisleri water unsafe due to the presence of chemicals that health agencies say may cause cancer.
In the second notice to Bisleri, dated August 12 ⁠and seen by Reuters, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) relayed its findings to the company and asked it to prohibit the sale of ‌the affected batch, citing the presence of bacteria.
“The sample was found to be nonconforming [UNSAFE],” the notice said. “It shows presence of coliform.”
The sample was tested again for confirmation and was still found unsafe, said a government official, who declined ‌to be named as the results were not public.
Bisleri said it had 130 operational ⁠plants making its products and 5,980 distributors. ⁠Multinational conglomerate Tata was previously in talks to acquire the bottler, which counts several Bollywood stars among brand ambassadors, including Deepika Padukone.
Mumbai-based Bisleri told Reuters in a statement on Saturday that it ‌had recalled the batch in August on the government’s instructions and that “the primary and referral laboratories reported the presence of coliform bacteria in the regulatory sample”.
But the company said it commissioned independent testing ‌of samples from ‌the same batch, which found they met “the applicable standard for coliform bacteria and all other applicable food safety standards”.
A shopkeeper moves Bisleri packaged drinking water bottles at a shop in Kolkata, India. Photo: Reuters
“The difference between the regulatory and ‌independent findings warrants a thorough review,” the company said. “Bisleri will continue to cooperate fully with FSSAI to establish the facts.”
The regulator did not immediately respond to ⁠a request for comment.
Reuters reported on Monday that the food regulator had asked all states to strengthen oversight and intensify surveillance of the packaged water industry ⁠in light of the Bisleri findings.
The agency ordered states to hold “regular inspections and risk-based sampling of packaged drinking water and mineral water”, saying “appropriate action shall be initiated in cases of non-compliance”.
The checks will increase regulatory oversight of PepsiCo, Tata Consumer, Coca-Cola and billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s ‌Reliance Consumer, which have all bet ‌on the sector.
In the first finding against Bisleri, court records show that the food regulator has initiated prosecution proceedings, which could include a jail term and fine for manufacturing a sample found unsafe.
Indian authorities have stepped up enforcement against major food and drinks brands in recent weeks. Federal and state regulators have conducted many raids and reprimanded companies for improper labelling, affecting everyone from Domino’s to Diageo.
The Supreme Court this week tightened proposed warning labels, in another setback for the US$100 billion industry.

title_en: Chinese engineers defy Hormuz blockade to install Abu Dhabi drilling rigs
content_en:
Workers from state-run Honghua Group brave shipping closures and drone strikes to deliver and assemble AI-enabled oil rigs in the UAE.
The oil rigs combine automation, artificial intelligence (AI), digital systems and hybrid power. Photo: Handout
As fighter jets screamed just above, a group of Chinese engineers defied wartime blockades in the Strait of Hormuz to deliver and install drilling rigs on an Abu Dhabi island.
A team from Honghua Group, a unit of state-owned Dongfang Electric Group, transited the strait into the Persian Gulf to deliver two AI-enabled drill rigs to Abu Dhabi earlier this year, and has since raised the derrick of a third, according to a report by China Electric Power News on Thursday.
“The smart drilling rigs were successfully installed amid volatile and unpredictable conditions,” said the newspaper overseen by China’s National Energy Administration.
The rigs are among six expected to be delivered to artificial islands in the offshore Zakum oilfield in the United Arab Emirates under two drilling services contracts valued at a combined US$1.54 billion.
ADNOC Drilling, the drilling arm of Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, said it had expected the first three rigs to arrive this year when the first contract was announced in July 2024.
But regional tensions posed challenges to delivery.
Honghua logistics coordinator Yang Xiaoli told the newspaper that the company had set up a dedicated response team after learning in February that its usual shipping route had been disrupted.
Earlier that month, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations office had advised ships to proceed with caution. Iran temporarily closed part of the strait on February 17.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted after the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28. Iran began blocking the strait that day and later, in March, said it would only allow “non-hostile” vessels to transit if they complied with its security requirements and coordinated with Iranian authorities.
Yang said the team spent days contacting shipping companies, insurers and local authorities before finding a local vessel that could transit the strait.
They then negotiated charter terms, arranged barges and vehicles to move the equipment to the island and secured the necessary clearances.
The shipment arrived on schedule.
Once the rigs reached the island, the team faced the risks of working near a war zone. On March 10, workers saw smoke from two explosions at sea about 10km (6 miles) away.
Minutes later, a local fighter jet shot down a drone about 2km from the island, the newspaper reported. The blast was heard at the site.
“The fighter jet suddenly accelerated, and the sonic boom was deafening,” Honghua safety officer He Jun told the newspaper. “There was a moment of panic. We immediately activated our emergency plan and organised an evacuation.”
A Chinese company is expected to deliver six drill rigs to artificial islands in the offshore Zakum oilfield in the United Arab Emirates. Photo: Handout
The official Emirates News Agency (WAM) reported that the country’s air defences had detected nine ballistic missiles that day. Eight were destroyed and one fell into the sea.
Of the 35 drones detected, 26 were intercepted and nine came down within the UAE, the report said.
“We grabbed hold of one another and called out as we ran to the safety zone,” He was quoted as saying.
With flights and boat services temporarily suspended over security concerns, the team recorded workers’ blood types and emergency contacts and asked them to pack evacuation bags with valuables and emergency supplies, according to China Electric Power News.
The team kept two boats on standby around the clock, arranged a shelter off the island and held repeated evacuation drills.
Other challenges included limited space, high temperatures and strong winds.
ADNOC Drilling announced on June 25 that it had accepted delivery of the first rig nearly three months ahead of schedule.
The second rig joined the company’s fleet in the third quarter and began operating around the end of September, the company said last month.
The company said the first rig, built by Honghua Group, combined automation, artificial intelligence (AI), digital systems and hybrid power.
In 2012, Honghua signed a contract with ADNOC Drilling to supply nine 3,000-horsepower artificial island rigs, which entered service in 2014.
By Eve Qiao

title_en: US military says cyber systems secure after reports of Air Force hack
content_en:
In recent weeks, the CIA and FBI, as well as suppliers for several big banks, were also reportedly subject to hacks.
A US Air Force fighter aircraft F-35 performs at an aerospace event in Bengaluru, India, in 2023. The Air Force has denied that its cloud-based system was hacked. Photo: AP
The US military denied on Friday any issues with its computer security following media reports that the Air Force’s cloud-based system was hacked, in what would be the latest high-profile breach of US digital infrastructure in recent weeks.
Asked whether the Air Force’s Cloud One platform had been hacked, the Pentagon did not specifically deny that the system had been breached.
Instead, a Defence Department official said late on Friday: “The Department of War’s systems are safe, secure, and managed 24-7 by the best experts and teams in the world. We will continue to maintain all mission-critical operations and applications.”
A Defence Department official said earlier on Friday: “As a matter of policy and operations security, the Department of War does not comment on the status of our networks.”
NBC News, a major US broadcaster, reported on Friday, citing an unnamed US official, that the cloud platform had been breached and that an attack “could have exposed sensitive military information”.
The breach was first reported by Reuters earlier on Friday.
Federal News Network, which specialises in covering US federal agencies, also confirmed the breach, citing a “person familiar with the incident”.
The contractors discovered the hack earlier in the year while doing maintenance on the system, Federal News said.
The reported attack is the latest in a string of major outages in US government and private-sector digital infrastructure.
The Central Intelligence Agency was reportedly hit by hacking recently. Photo: Shutterstock
In recent weeks, the CIA and FBI were also reportedly subject to hacks.
Suppliers for major American financial institutions, including JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard, were also hit.
In other instances, such as a major Microsoft Outlook outage, a separate US air traffic control issue and a reported issue with a top-secret National Security Agency network earlier this month, officials were at pains to blame the outages on maintenance or defects – not intrusions.
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base back in spotlight after Chinese radar features in joint drill
content_en:
The Chinese-funded base already faced intense scrutiny before the appearance of the long-range LCQ-776 at the Golden Dragon 2006 exercises.
The LCQ-776 air surveillance and early warning radar has featured in photos from the drill’s opening ceremony on November 25. Photo: Handout
Chinese-made long-range radar equipment has been spotted at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base during the ongoing Golden Dragon 2026 exercises, a move likely to draw fresh attention to the air surveillance capabilities at the Chinese-funded naval facility.
Photos and video released to local media showed an LCQ-776 air surveillance and early warning radar alongside Cambodian troops and mounted on a truck with a Royal Cambodian Armed Forces licence plate.
It remains unclear whether this indicates the system has been transferred to the Cambodian military or is only there for the joint exercise with the Chinese military, which will run until December 9.
They are the first known pictures of the radar taken in Cambodia and follow years of speculation about surveillance equipment at the base. The system is capable of tracking aircraft up to 500km (310 miles) away.
If installed at Ream, the 3D radar would be able to monitor parts of neighbouring Thailand and Vietnam as well as the surrounding waters.
[embedded media]
Situated on the Gulf of Thailand, Ream Naval Base – one of three venues for this year’s exercises – has undergone extensive Chinese-funded expansion and modernisation in recent years.
In recent years, Beijing’s increasing presence at the strategically located base near the southern tip of Cambodia, close to the South China Sea, has fuelled Western concerns that China is seeking a military outpost in the region.
Cambodia has offered other navies access to the facility to dispel suspicions that it is giving China exclusive use and has denied that it hosts a Chinese base.
In 2023, the Cambodian military acquired a Chinese-made KS-1C surface-to-air missile system, which has a range of up to 70km, according to media reports.
Pairing long-range aerial tracking with Cambodia’s existing KS-1C batteries would effectively close a major gap in the country’s air-defence network.
“The installation of radars covering Cambodia’s air and maritime domains is particularly important,” Abdul Rahman Yaacob, then a research fellow at Australia’s Lowy Institute, wrote in a 2024 analysis.
He added that the radar would help the country’s military enhance its maritime domain awareness, detect potential air and sea threats, and protect commercial shipping.
Other images from the exercise’s opening ceremony on Wednesday showed Chinese hardware, including Type 96A battle tanks.
The joint drills are the largest held so far and will run until December 9. Photo: Handout
The 15-day exercise involves 2,940 troops – including around 1,300 People’s Liberation Army personnel – and is the largest of the eight held since the Golden Dragon drills began in 2016.
This year’s exercises will focus on security threats such as terrorism and piracy, alongside humanitarian assistance, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua.
It added that the exercises were not targeting any third party or linked to regional dynamics or sensitive issues.
The PLA Air Force said on Thursday it would put its next-generation early warning radar on static display for the first time at the coming Zhuhai air show in early December, without disclosing further details.
By Amber Wang

title_en: Costa Rica bars UN-picked human rights expert on Palestinian territories
content_en:
Under President Laura Fernandez, Costa Rica has deepened cooperation with the United States on security and has ‌moved closer to Israel.
Police stand guard outside the Costa Rican embassy in Mexico City on Friday after Costa Rica denied entry to Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory. Photo: Reuters
Costa Rica denied entry ⁠to the United Nations special rapporteur on ⁠the Israeli-occupied Palestinian territories, drawing criticism from UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday.
Costa Rica’s move put the small Central American country’s increasingly close alignment with Washington and Israel on security and foreign policy into the spotlight.
Turk said he was “deeply concerned” by Costa Rica’s ‌decision to bar Francesca Albanese from entering the country and urged authorities to reconsider after she was stopped at Juan Santamaria airport, which serves the capital San Jose.
Albanese, an Italian national, had travelled to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the state-run University of Costa Rica. A UN special rapporteur is an independent expert appointed by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate and report on ⁠rights abuses in a specific country.
The UN human rights office said on social media that Albanese was denied entry ‌on “claimed national security grounds”. Costa Rica’s migration office said it had acted after receiving an alert and that the decision was consistent with national security measures.
On Friday evening, Costa ‌Rican authorities allowed Albanese to be transferred to a hotel near the San Jose airport to ⁠spend the night before ⁠she travels to Mexico on Saturday.
UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese shown on a screen during a ceremony at the University of Costa Rica in San Jose on Friday. Photo: EPA
Costa Rica, under President Laura Fernandez, has deepened cooperation with the United States on security and has ‌moved closer to Israel, a notable shift for a country long associated with support for multilateral institutions.
Albanese, who has been sanctioned by the United ‌States ‌under measures related to the International Criminal Court, said she hoped Costa Rica would reverse the decision and ‌rejected what she described as efforts to link her to terrorism.
In a video call interview with journalist Ahmed ⁠Shihab-Eldin recorded from a gate at the airport, Albanese said authorities took her passport and that she was offered ⁠a detention room to sleep in that was so smelly she almost became ill.
“I was almost forced to board the plane to be shipped back to Paris. I said no, and ‌I opposed it … and they ‌threatened to put me on the plane by force,” she said.
Albanese has become one of the most outspoken international critics of Israel’s conduct in Gaza, making her a frequent target of pro-Israel officials and governments. Israel’s UN ambassador, Danny Danon, praised Costa Rica’s decision in a social media post.
By Reuters

Albanese, who has been sanctioned by the United ‌States ‌under measures related to the International Criminal Court, said she hoped Costa Rica would reverse the decision and ‌rejected what she described as efforts to link her to terrorism.

title_en: Japan’s airlines brace for looming ‘2030 problem’: pilot shortages
content_en:
Apart from a large pool of pilots set to retire around 2030, Japan’s greying population means airlines may face problems hiring replacements.
All Nippon Airways and Japan Airlines planes at Haneda airport in Tokyo. Photo: Kyodo
Japan’s aviation industry is set to face a severe shortage of pilots – dubbed the “2030 problem” – as more long-serving crew members retire in the next few years and demand in the tourism sector continues to rise.
The nation’s major airlines say they are taking steps to ensure there are no disruptions to services by stepping up pilot training and recruitment. Analysts warn that while the global aviation industry is experiencing similar headwinds, Japan’s pool of potential pilots is expected to shrink because of its greying population.
Should Japan Airlines (JAL), All Nippon Airways (ANA) and other domestic carriers fail to recruit more pilots, they may have to start reducing services, potentially affecting their partner airlines flying across the Asia-Pacific region, according to analysts.
JAL and ANA – Japan’s two leading airlines – expanded their operations during the country’s “bubble economy” of the late 1980s and early 1990s, particularly on international routes to Europe and North America. Many pilots hired during that boom are approaching the mandatory retirement age of 65 around 2030, driving the looming crunch.
“The issue of a shortage of commercial pilots is not just Japan-specific; it’s a global issue,” said Toshimitsu Sogabe, an aviation industry analyst in the Tokyo office of Cirium Ascend Consultancy.
“It has been a problem since the aviation market recovered from the global pandemic, and a lot of the pilots who had not been flying did not want to come back. There had been a lot of changes in the industry, and airlines had to train people quickly,” Sogabe said.
While “the global market eventually sorted itself out”, every sector in Japan was facing labour shortages amid the shrinking population, he added.
Tourists visiting the Sensoji Temple in Tokyo. Foreign tourist arrivals in Japan continue to rise this year, spurring demand for flights by domestic airlines. Photo: EPA
According to Sogabe, hiring pilots is expensive, and their training takes a long time, with Japanese airlines partnering specialist flight training companies in the US and elsewhere.
The training process to obtain a basic pilot qualification typically takes more than three years, while further training to fly certain larger aircraft takes a year for each model. Airlines generally expect a minimum of 10 years’ service before a first officer is promoted to captain of an aircraft.
On Wednesday, ANA Holdings announced it was setting up a subsidiary, ANA Next Aviation, to conduct basic pilot training in-house – the first such training company established by a Japanese airline. Based at Kagoshima Airport in southern Japan, it is scheduled to begin training operations in the second half of the 2027 financial year.
An ANA spokesman said the airline currently had sufficient employees for operations, downplaying concerns over the impact of the looming pilot shortage.
“We view the ‘2030 problem’ as a key turning point to pass on our veteran employees’ expertise to the next generation, and we are taking proactive steps to ensure sustainable growth,” said the spokesman, who declined to be named.
“Alongside expanding recruitment and extending the retirement age, we recently established ANA Next Aviation … to build a stable in-house training pipeline from basic to aircraft training.”
He said ANA did not anticipate having to cut services or halt routes if crew shortages were to become acute, and that it was “preparing well for the ‘2030 problem’”.
A JAL spokesman said the airline had also been taking measures, including increasing recruitment and hiring foreign pilots.
Passengers gathering at the departure hall in Kansai International Airport in Osaka prefecture. Photo: AFP
“At this time, we do not anticipate any reductions in flight frequency or route suspensions,” he said, but refused to comment on the likelihood of changes to flight frequency or fares, or on connectivity with JAL’s partner airlines in the region and beyond.
Sogabe said the airline sector was not just facing a chronic labour shortage, but also high aviation fuel prices.
He added that Japanese authorities might have to consider raising the retirement age for pilots eventually while ensuring they could pass the relevant safety tests.
In the meantime, Japanese airlines may have to revamp their operations, including increasing routes on the more profitable international routes to help offset the impact of a weak yen and consolidating their services, according to Sogabe.
“I suspect some operations may have to be consolidated, with domestic services most at risk as this part of their operations is losing money right now. With costs so high, it is only natural for airlines to consolidate routes or to outsource some of their operations to regional airlines using smaller aircraft,” he said.
By Julian Ryall
