title_en: Chinese wife asks online gamers to repeatedly ‘kill’ husband to curb late-night gaming habit
content_en:
Even World of Warcraft’s official Chinese account joined in, posting a video joking about ‘the wife’s bounty on her husband’.
A Chinese woman recruited online gamers to repeatedly defeat her husband in a game to break his late-night habit. Photo: Shutterstock
A woman in southern China’s Guangdong province called on gamers to “kill” her husband in an online game to stop him staying up all night playing the game. Her plan worked after numerous players joined the hunt.
The woman, surnamed Chen, posted a video on November 14 showing her husband, surnamed Li, playing the online game. She asked other players to “kill” him at around 1am so he would come to bed with her.
Chen said Li had stayed up playing until 3 or 4am for the previous three nights, disturbing her sleep.
Many netizens initially took her request as a joke. But Li’s response in the video soon changed their minds. Ignoring Chen’s plea for help, he confidently declared that it was “impossible for them to find him.”
“I wasn’t going to help your wife, but you’ve given me a good reason to hunt you down,” one player commented.
The video revealed Li’s in-game ID, “tiantiankaixin” – Chinese for “happy every day” – as well as his location and character.
Chen said her husband, above, had stayed up gaming until 3 or 4am for three nights in a row, disrupting her sleep. Photo: douyin
Over the following nights, numerous players logged into the game with one mission: to find and kill “tiantiankaixin.” During one three-hour stretch, Li was repeatedly killed. Each time, he had to make a “corpse run” – running as a spirit from a graveyard back to the place where his character had died so he could resurrect.
On the second night after Chen posted her appeal, Li went to bed before midnight. Chen said it was the earliest he had gone to sleep all year.
Other players using the same ID, “tiantiankaixin,” were also mistakenly targeted.
Some joked that “tiantiankaixin” had become an Easter egg – or a hidden boss – in the game. One player quipped: “‘Tiantiankaixin’ has become ‘tiantianxintong’” – a play on words meaning “heartbroken every day.”
Another commenter took a more serious tone: “I support the wife’s request. He has the freedom playing games, but staying up late to play is very harmful to his health.”
The World Health Organization officially recognises severe gaming addiction — known as gaming disorder — as a mental health condition. Photo: EPA-EFE/Wu Hao
On the fourth day, Chen said Li had switched to a character with an invisible mode, but players continued to report his location and hunt him down.
Even World of Warcraft’s official Chinese account posted a video joking about “the wife’s bounty on her husband.”
Li has reportedly since stopped staying up late to play online games.
The World Health Organization formally included gaming disorder in the 11th Revision of the International Classification of Diseases in 2019, prompting changes in public health policy and clinical practice related to gaming addiction in China.
Li’s gaming habits do not appear severe enough to meet the criteria for gaming disorder. However, doctors have warned that staying up late can pose health risks, including sleep problems and memory loss, and, in more serious cases, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases.
By Fran Lu

title_en: Australia quietly revives Antarctic logistics pact with China as ties steady
content_en:
The deal covering aviation, ground transport and emergency support for 2026–27 follows a one-year gap in cooperation.
The Chinese research icebreaker Xuelong sails towards a port near Hobart, Australia on November 18, 2026. The Australian city is an important gateway to Antarctica. Photo: Xinhua
Australia has quietly revived a bilateral Antarctic logistics pact with China, as the two countries work to put bilateral ties on a stable footing despite lingering security tensions.
The new agreement, which covers logistics cooperation for the 2026-27 Antarctic summer season, was revealed in an Australian Senate estimates brief prepared for the environment department last month and obtained by the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) under freedom of information laws, the public broadcaster reported on Friday.
The agreement had since been enacted, the report said, quoting the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT).
While details were not disclosed, the deal is a “quid pro quo” arrangement allowing reciprocal support for operations, including aviation, ground transport and emergency help – mirroring previous pacts the two countries signed for 2019-20, 2023-24 and 2024-25, according to the report.
“Australia and China have a long-standing collaborative relationship on Antarctic matters, including logistical cooperation, the specific nature of which varies season to season,” the report quoted DFAT as saying, without explaining the gap in 2025-26.
Australia is trying to strengthen economic ties with China, its largest trading partner, following a years-long trade war that ended in 2024. Canberra’s efforts to improve relations were highlighted by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s visit to Shenzhen and Beijing last week.
[embedded media]
Canberra and Beijing have worked together in Antarctic research for decades.
During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Australia in 2014, the two countries signed a pact aimed at expanding practical collaboration in the field.
The Chinese icebreaker Xuelong docked at Hobart last week to refuel and load supplies before heading to Antarctica.
“I look forward to continued cooperation in Antarctic scientific research and exploration,” said Wang Yu, China’s consul general in Sydney, on social media on November 19.
The Polar Research Institute of China announced on November 16 that it had recently discussed cooperation in “air transport, personnel deployment, supply of materials, port services and polar equipment support” with a visiting delegation led by Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff.
However, the China-Australia relationship has been strained in security and defence amid intense competition in the Pacific, underscored by the Solomon Islands’ recent decision to replace its 2022 security pact with Beijing with a sweeping new treaty with Canberra.
According to the ABC report, the estimates brief also mentioned China’s expanding presence in Antarctica, which includes plans for a sixth research station and has raised security concerns among observers in Australia.
While Beijing has not made any high-profile announcements about the project, state news agency Xinhua noted in a report in early November on China’s 43rd Antarctic expedition that its tasks included preliminary site surveys and mapping for supporting facilities at the planned Marie Byrd Land station.
Under the Antarctic Treaty, which has 58 parties, signatory nations are free to build research stations and facilities anywhere on the continent for peaceful scientific purposes.
The ABC report also noted that the estimates brief had flagged China’s planned ice runway for large aircraft.
The proposed project features a blue-ice runway measuring 4,000 metres (13,120 feet) long and 60 metres wide, along with ground support facilities near Mason Peak in East Antarctica’s Princess Elizabeth Land, according to an initial environmental evaluation posted by China on the Secretariat of the Antarctic Treaty’s website late last year.
Construction of the runway is set to begin during the 2026-27 season, and it is expected to open in the 2029-30 austral summer. It will accommodate large intercontinental wheeled aircraft such as the Airbus A330-200, carrying up to 30 passengers and 15 tonnes of cargo per flight.
“[This] infrastructure will enable more efficient and convenient services for scientific expeditions and emergency support or rescue operations in East Antarctica,” the environmental report said.
With the planned runway falling within territory claimed by Australia, the ABC asked DFAT whether Canberra supported the project or had any concerns about it.
“Australia expects all parties to comply with the requirements of the Antarctic Treaty and its Environmental Protocol, including non-militarisation, freedom of scientific investigation, international cooperation, environmental protection and the mining ban,” the department said.
Australia is one of seven nations claiming territory in Antarctica, although the Antarctic Treaty freezes all sovereignty claims, and other countries, including China, do not recognise any claims on the continent.
Additional reporting by Orange Wang
By Carol Yang

title_en: Myanmar’s Asean exit talk: a pariah pushes back
content_en:
Five years after his coup, Min Aung Hlaing shrugs off a UN genocide ruling and hints at leaving the bloc that excluded him.
Illustration: Huy Truong
For five years, one name card has been missing from the grand circular table at the Association of Southeast Asean Nations biannual leaders’ summit: Min Aung Hlaing.
As president of Myanmar, he should by diplomatic convention sit alongside the 10 other leaders of the Southeast Asian bloc at its regular get-togethers.
Yet Asean has kept Myanmar at arm’s length ever since the coup that Min Aung Hlaing led as army chief in February 2021.
At its latest summit in Manila this month, Myanmar was represented by Han Win Aung, a senior civil servant with the foreign ministry.
Min Aung Hlaing appears to be bristling at his continued diplomatic exclusion. In recent months, he has visited Bangkok, Hanoi and Kuala Lumpur, as well as New Delhi, Moscow and Beijing, in an effort to cast off his coup-leader past and emerge a legitimate head of state.
Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing waves as he leaves after delivering a speech to parliament in Naypyidaw on November 18. Photo: AP
On November 18 – a day before the UN’s top court found that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya population with its military operations in 2017 – the notoriously stubborn leader said he would “review” Myanmar’s relationship with Asean, complaining that no other member state had had to suffer such an “indignity”.
“They are imposing such pressure only on our country,” Min Aung Hlaing told parliament. “There was never pressure placed on or indignity shown towards an Asean member before. But with Myanmar, they are doing that.”
Days later, state media quoted him telling a government meeting that Myanmar would not comply with those parts of the International Court of Justice’s genocide ruling that it considered “inappropriate”, calling it a “one-sided accusation” that had “seriously affected” the country’s reputation.
Judges deliver a reading of the ICJ’s judgment in the genocide case brought against Myanmar at the Peace Palace in The Hague, Netherlands, on November 19. Photo: EPA
The ICJ found in its ruling on November 19 that at least 10,000 Rohingya civilians, a mostly Muslim minority group, had been killed by Myanmar’s security forces during the “clearance operations” of 2017.
Min Aung Hlaing was commander-in-chief of Myanmar’s military in 2017, a post he held until March this year, shortly before assuming the presidency.
In one such operation in August 2017, the court found that the military had “engaged in the indiscriminate and targeted killing of civilians, including children and persons fleeing; separated and executed men; committed widespread sexual violence; and burned people, bodies and homes”.
Chaos as leverage
Myanmar is far from the first Asean member to experience a military takeover or bouts of violent political turmoil. It is, however, the first to have been found responsible for genocide by the principal judicial organ of the United Nations.
In his remarks to parliament this month, Min Aung Hlaing stopped short of threatening to leave the regional bloc that his country only joined in 1997 – when it was, as now, under de facto military rule.
But as his 2021 coup showed, Myanmar’s president is unafraid of sowing chaos, and analysts say Asean should not be surprised if he and his military-dominated, rubber-stamp parliament decide to take another all-or-nothing gamble.
“If Myanmar left, it would only highlight the bloc’s inability to address serious problems,” said Lucas Myers, a Myanmar researcher and assistant director at the University of Maryland’s School of Public Policy, citing the country’s coup and ensuing deadly civil war as examples of “a series of crises to its [Asean’s] credibility”.
“In that sense, Naypyidaw has leverage that Asean does not,” he said.
The seat reserved for Myanmar is left empty during a meeting at the 43rd Asean Summit in Jakarta, Indonesia, in September 2023. Photo: Reuters
Asean bars Myanmar from sending political leaders to its summits until it makes progress on a peace plan, the “five-point consensus”, that was agreed two months after the coup. It calls for an immediate end to violence, constructive dialogue among all parties and humanitarian access.
Yet in the years since Min Aung Hlaing seized power, mass protests have been met with live fire; homes, hospitals, displacement camps and schools have been bombed; and dissidents – including Aung San Suu Kyi, the figurehead of Myanmar’s brief democratic opening – have been jailed.
Witnesses have provided “horrific accounts of sexual and gender-based crimes, torture, strangulation and electrocution” in detention, according to UN investigators. A UN committee heard last month that more than 100,000 people had been killed in the post-coup conflict, “the vast majority … civilians”.
At their summit in Manila on November 15, Asean leaders restated their “deep concern” over the humanitarian situation in Myanmar, denounced the violence and urged the military to stop its targeted attacks on “civilians and civilian infrastructure”.
They also endorsed “calibrated engagement” – a phrase coined by Thai diplomats this year amid Thailand’s efforts to act as a diplomatic bridge – and pledged to “consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation” subject to sustained and concrete progress on the five-point consensus’ implementation.
Asean’s charter commits its members to non-interference in each other’s domestic affairs. Rights groups say this has left the bloc largely powerless to curb violence by one of its own.
[embedded media]
Meanwhile, drugs and arms trafficking – plus scam gangs committing industrial-scale online fraud – have proliferated amid the instability, spilling out of Myanmar’s borders into its neighbours’ territory.
A conscription order has driven tens of thousands of young people to flee the country, many to Thailand and Malaysia, where they provide labour but also add strain to already overstretched public services, fuelling anti-immigrant sentiment.
Myers said that Asean’s priority, in contrast to Myanmar’s, was first and foremost to maintain unity among its members.
“Asean’s incentives as an institution are to hold together with the appearance – if not the reality – of harmony,” he said.
“Min Aung Hlaing simply wants to preserve and consolidate his personal control over the regime. He doesn’t need Asean to do that when he can go to Bangkok, Beijing and Moscow.”
‘Toxic and divisive’

title_en: Son of Hamas chief survived Israeli strike, group says
content_en:
Izzeldeen al-Hayya is the last surviving son of Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya.
A building where the family of Izzeldeen al-Hayya, son of Hamas chief Khalil al-Hayya, was reportedly staying is seen on Friday after it was hit in an Israeli air strike. Photo: Reuters
The son of Hamas ⁠chief Khalil al-Hayya survived an assassination attempt ⁠by the Israeli military on Friday, senior Hamas official ⁠Basem Naim said.
He said that Izzeldeen al-Hayya and his family had survived a dawn air strike and Hamas sources said several people, including Hayya’s daughter-in-law, had been wounded but there had been no deaths.
The Israeli military had no immediate comment.
Naim described Izzeldeen al-Hayya, born in 1997, as the Hamas chief’s last surviving son, with four others ‌having been killed by Israeli forces.
The family of one of the late sons survived Friday’s strike, Naim said.
Hamas’ Khalil al-Hayya waits to cross into Egypt through the Rafah border crossing in February 2021. Photo: dpa
Hamas said in a statement that the Israeli military had targeted a residential apartment, and linked the attack to threats Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has made against Hayya.
Hamas accused Israel of seeking to undermine a 2025 Gaza ceasefire agreement and said Israel bore full responsibility for the consequences of its continued attacks.
Izzeldeen is the twin brother of Hamam Khalil al-Hayya, who was killed in a 2025 ⁠Israeli air strike targeting Hamas leaders in Qatar, Naim said.
Named Hamas’ overall leader in July, Hayya narrowly escaped assassination himself in the Qatar strike.
Hayya warned of possible retaliation on Thursday after Israeli attacks killed at least 10 people in Gaza.
Two separate Israeli strikes killed five Palestinians in Gaza on Friday, medical workers said.
The first strike killed three Palestinians ‌and wounded two in the city of Rafah, medical sources said. The Israeli military spokesman said the military had ⁠struck three militants without giving ⁠further information.
In the second attack, Palestinian medical staff said the two people, who worked as civil guards at an office of the Medecins Sans Frontieres in Gaza City, were ‌killed.
MSF confirmed that the two men were watchmen at the organisation, calling for accountability over the attack. It said the total number of its workers killed in Gaza reached ‌17.
A Palestinian man inspects a vehicle damaged by shrapnel from a projectile following an Israeli air strike that targeted a residential apartment where the family of Izzeldeen al-Hayya was staying. Photo: Reuters
The Israeli military acknowledged the two men worked for MSF, describing them as Hamas militants who were “posing as humanitarian workers”.
Israel has continued ‌to carry out attacks it says target Hamas, but the attacks have also killed many civilians. The broader ceasefire plan, backed by US President ⁠Donald Trump, has not halted the violence or secured Hamas’ disarmament.
At least 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers have been killed since ⁠the ceasefire was agreed to in October 2025, according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies.
Israeli troops control around two-thirds of Gaza, up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire, while Hamas controls a thin piece of territory along ‌Gaza’s coast.
Israel’s assault on Gaza ‌has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since 2023, caused a hunger crisis, internally displaced Gaza’s entire population and led to assessments of genocide from scholars and a United Nations inquiry.
Israel has denied the allegations of genocide, saying it acted in self-defence after Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took more than 250 hostages in an attack on Israel in October 2023.
By Reuters

title_en: DeepSeek is China’s latest developer to worry about losing control of AI
content_en:
Third-party evaluation finds safety gains in Chinese start-up’s flagship model, though open-weight safeguards can still be bypassed.
DeepSeek is the latest Chinese AI company to turn to external expertise as concerns mount globally over increasingly powerful AI systems. Photo: Shutterstock
Chinese artificial intelligence start-up DeepSeek has commissioned a third-party evaluation to assess whether its flagship model, V4 Pro, could escape human control, making it the latest Chinese AI developer to signal its concerns with the growing risks surrounding the technology.
The evaluation, published on Wednesday by Beijing-based AI safety consultancy Concordia AI, concluded that the model showed “limited ability” to replicate itself or deceive its human creators, though it resisted attempts to be shut down in some instances.
“The report offers evidence to support developers, deployers, researchers and policymakers in understanding and managing frontier AI risks,” Concordia’s researchers wrote.
Hangzhou-based DeepSeek is the latest Chinese AI company to turn to external expertise as concerns mount globally over increasingly powerful AI systems.
Earlier this month, Tencent Holdings partnered with Israeli-American AI safety start-up Alice and Beijing-based Fangcun AI to assess the risks of its latest Hy4 model before releasing it as open-weight software.
In September, Concordia worked with GLM developer Z.ai — also known as Zhipu AI — on a risk management framework related to the risks of open-weight AI models. Concordia has also signed official partnership agreements with DeepSeek, MiniMax and Huawei Technologies.
“The independence of third parties is key in raising trust in evaluation results and helps bring more mature risk management across the industry,” said Cheng Yuan, senior manager for AI safety and governance at Concordia.
Concordia’s latest report concluded that DeepSeek’s V4 Pro 0813, released in August, showed substantial safety improvements over a previous version released in April. The findings cover five risk categories, including cyberattacks, biological and chemical risks, harmful manipulation and loss of human control.
However, the researchers warned that these safety gains relied on safeguards that could be circumvented by malicious actors with enough technical know-how, underscoring the risks of deploying powerful models as open-weight systems.
Most leading Chinese models are open-weight, meaning that users can download and modify the underlying technology, unlike closed US models.
[embedded media]
According to Concordia, DeepSeek commissioned its latest evaluation but agreed not to review, revise or veto its findings. DeepSeek did not respond to a request for comment.
Beijing and Washington have agreed to collaborate on AI risks in recent months, with AI model evaluations emerging as an early area of discussion.
Earlier this month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two countries would share approaches for evaluating advanced AI models before they are released at Shenzhen’s Apec summit. However, neither side mentioned such discussions in their post-summit readouts, amid growing tensions over US tech restrictions on China.
The push to collaborate comes as Beijing warned that frontier AI models were “showing signs of escaping human control”, which could “threaten human survival”, earlier this month.
Such official concerns have prompted greater efforts in China to evaluate AI models for their frontier risks.
Another report published on Wednesday by researchers at Shanghai’s Fudan University concluded that leading Chinese and Western models, including those from DeepSeek, Z.ai and Meta Platforms, were showing signs of “evaluation awareness”, where they recognised they were being safety tested.
Experts have warned that this would undermine the reliability of safety tests for predicting real-world behaviour.
Such concerns continue to mount in the US as well, with Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman stressing the importance of humans remaining in control of AI in a social media post on Wednesday.
“We are crossing a threshold. Safety and alignment work is the only thing that matters,” Suleyman wrote.

“The independence of third parties is key in raising trust in evaluation results and helps bring more mature risk management across the industry,” said Cheng Yuan, senior manager for AI safety and governance at Concordia.
Concordia’s latest report concluded that DeepSeek’s V4 Pro 0813, released in August, showed substantial safety improvements over a previous version released in April. The findings cover five risk categories, including cyberattacks, biological and chemical risks, harmful manipulation and loss of human control.
However, the researchers warned that these safety gains relied on safeguards that could be circumvented by malicious actors with enough technical know-how, underscoring the risks of deploying powerful models as open-weight systems.
Most leading Chinese models are open-weight, meaning that users can download and modify the underlying technology, unlike closed US models.

According to Concordia, DeepSeek commissioned its latest evaluation but agreed not to review, revise or veto its findings. DeepSeek did not respond to a request for comment.
Beijing and Washington have agreed to collaborate on AI risks in recent months, with AI model evaluations emerging as an early area of discussion.
Earlier this month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two countries would share approaches for evaluating advanced AI models before they are released at Shenzhen’s Apec summit. However, neither side mentioned such discussions in their post-summit readouts, amid growing tensions over US tech restrictions on China.
The push to collaborate comes as Beijing warned that frontier AI models were “showing signs of escaping human control”, which could “threaten human survival”, earlier this month.
Such official concerns have prompted greater efforts in China to evaluate AI models for their frontier risks.
Another report published on Wednesday by researchers at Shanghai’s Fudan University concluded that leading Chinese and Western models, including those from DeepSeek, Z.ai and Meta Platforms, were showing signs of “evaluation awareness”, where they recognised they were being safety tested.
Experts have warned that this would undermine the reliability of safety tests for predicting real-world behaviour.
Such concerns continue to mount in the US as well, with Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman stressing the importance of humans remaining in control of AI in a social media post on Wednesday.
“We are crossing a threshold. Safety and alignment work is the only thing that matters,” Suleyman wrote.
